title: The question and the answer
show: The sentence under the title, and the four figures beneath it.
say: This is the study we submitted to the Quantum Hackathon with Bloq. The question: can a quantum-kernel support vector machine predict death in heart-failure patients as well as classical models? Everything on this page is computed from the files we submitted, nothing is typed in. The answer is in the sentence: on {{n_train}} training patients the best quantum kernel and the best classical model are tied, {{q_mcc}} against {{c_mcc}} on MCC. I will now show how every number was checked.

title: The six experiments
show: The table of E1 to E6. The last column is the re-check status. Row E5 opens to show its claims.
say: E1 and E2 ran on the Bloq platform and came out near zero. E3 and E4 are local sweeps I ran to understand why. E5 is the file we submitted. E6 is a stricter local benchmark we did not submit. The new part is the right-hand column: code re-ran each row and says whether its numbers reproduce.

title: Why the platform runs collapsed
show: Bloq settings and confusion matrices, then the range chart and the platform-gap box.
say: On Bloq, the default ZZ feature map with four qubits gave MCC {{e1_mcc}} without time and {{e2_mcc}} with time, close to no skill. My first explanation was kernel concentration at large input ranges. The sweep confirms that effect: at range zero to two pi the cross-validated MCC falls to {{e3_2pi}}. But I tested the other half. With inputs in zero to one, our local ZZ kernel never predicted no-deaths in {{gap_n}} random splits. So split luck does not explain the platform result, and whether Bloq rescales inputs internally cannot be checked from outside. I label that a hypothesis.

title: Every claim, recomputed
show: The claim table with a status for each row.
say: Here is every claim from our report, the value we recomputed, and a status. {{n_hold}} of {{n_claims}} hold. The submitted QSVM holdout MCC of {{hold_mcc}} reproduces exactly, with the same confusion matrix. It reproduces with an angle-embedding kernel, which has no entanglement. A true ZZ kernel on the same inputs gives {{zz_same}}, so the file's feature-map label had to be corrected. Some things did not reproduce: the tree-model baselines and one cross-validation fold. And one claim, that the run happened on Bloq, cannot be verified by any tool outside the platform.

title: The holdout is fragile
show: Sixty dots, one per patient. Grey is correct, red is an error. Clicking a dot flips that prediction.
say: The holdout is only {{n_test}} patients. Each dot is one patient. There are {{n_err}} errors in red. Watch the MCC when I flip one prediction. One flipped patient moves it between {{one_min}} and {{one_max}}, two between {{two_min}} and {{two_max}}. So gaps of a few hundredths on this holdout are noise. That is why I chose the input range by cross-validation, not by the holdout.

title: Fair comparison
show: The interval plot for repeated cross-validation, then the Honesty Guard verdict.
say: For a fair comparison I ran all eight models on the same {{n_splits}} paired splits and gave the scores to the QNeuro Forge Honesty Guard. It uses a corrected resampled t-test, because cross-validation folds overlap, and it corrects for the {{configs}} quantum configurations I tried. The verdict is {{verdict_cat}}. The best quantum kernel scored {{q_mcc}} and the best classical model {{c_mcc}}. The guard is the only code allowed to word a quantum advantage claim, and here it declines to.

title: Follow-up time
show: Single-feature scores, then with-time versus without-time for four models.
say: The track allows follow-up time as a feature. It carries outcome information: alone it scores AUROC {{time_auc}}, higher than any other single feature. Swapping it for serum sodium lowers cross-validated MCC for every model, by {{drop_min}} to {{drop_max}}. So the with-time numbers are optimistic for a model that has to predict before follow-up exists. Our report listed this comparison as future work. I ran it locally here, not on Bloq.

title: What was edited before submission
show: The three-row diff between the Bloq export and the submitted file.
say: Before submitting, we corrected three text fields in the Bloq export: the feature-map name, a leakage note and a verdict sentence. This diff is computed from the two files. Every number is identical. The original note claimed time inflates MCC across models, which the file had never tested, and it called the kernel a ZZ map although it behaves as a product-state kernel.

title: Verify in the browser, then break it
show: The artifact table. First every hash is checked, then one byte is corrupted.
say: Every input and output file has a SHA-256 hash in a signed manifest. This button recomputes each hash in your browser. Now I corrupt one byte of the submitted file in memory and check again. Verification fails for exactly that file and for nothing else.

title: Signature and audit chain
show: Signature facts, then the audit chain table.
say: The whole study is signed with ML-DSA-65, a NIST post-quantum signature standard, and every step is recorded in a hash-chained log of {{audit_entries}} entries, each signed. The browser can recompute hashes but not check this signature. The command line can. Switch to the terminal now.

title: Limits and next steps
say: What this does not show. No hardware run: everything is a simulator. A 60-patient holdout. We cannot verify from outside that E5 ran on Bloq. The post-quantum libraries are unaudited demonstration code. And this is research tooling, not a diagnostic tool. Next steps: run the no-time comparison on the platform, lock a holdout, and try hardware.
